# Bowel surgery

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Bowel surgery*

[Original Article Link](/library/Cl0q_T)

---

## Summary

Bowel <u>surgery</u> encompasses all surgical procedures of the small and <u>large intestine</u>. The underlying conditions most commonly requiring bowel <u>surgery</u> are malignancies (especially <u>colorectal cancer</u>) and inflammatory processes (e.g., sigmoid <u>diverticulitis</u>). These surgical procedures may require the creation of an <u>artificial bowel outlet</u> (<u>stoma</u>). Depending on the underlying disease process and the planned surgical procedures, a <u>stoma</u> may be temporary or permanent. A permanent <u>stoma</u> is created following a procedure in which continence could not be preserved, whereas a temporary <u>stoma</u> allows for uninterrupted bowel healing (e.g., following <u>surgery</u>). Intestinal stomas are usually loop stomas, consisting of a <u>proximal</u> and a <u>distal</u> end, while end stomas have one opening which functions as an <u>artificial anus</u>. Major <u>complications of bowel surgery</u> include <u>anastomosis insufficiency</u>, which may lead to <u>abscess</u> formation, <u>peritonitis</u>, and <u>sepsis</u>, and <u>fascial dehiscence</u>, which may lead to <u>organ evisceration</u> and <u>incisional hernias</u>. Common <u>stoma</u> complications include <u>skin</u> irritation and <u>dehydration</u> secondary to high output. <u>Bariatric surgery</u> is an effective treatment for weight loss in patients with <u>obesity</u> and <u>metabolic syndrome</u>. Common complications associated with the procedure include <u>dumping syndrome</u>, strictures, and <u>internal hernias</u>.




Further bowel <u>surgery</u> techniques such as left and <u>right hemicolectomy</u>, transverse <u>colectomy</u>, <u>proctocolectomy</u>, and <u>ileal pouch-anal anastomosis</u> are discussed in the articles on <u>colorectal cancer</u> and <u>ulcerative colitis</u>.

---

## Technique/steps

### Basic surgical approaches




Bowel <u>surgery</u> can either be performed laparoscopically or as a conventional open procedure. The creation of an <u>artificial bowel outlet</u> or <u>stoma</u> (see below) may be necessary.




![Important abdominal and inguinal incision sites and potential indications](media/jv0oynzi98s1ogav0e2eyza7.jpg)

Important abdominal and inguinal incision sites and potential indications




### Elective <u>surgery</u>




The following factors can help maximize surgical <u>efficacy</u> in planned procedures:




* Time <u>surgery</u> to take place in periods in which possible inflammation is absent or low.

* Optimum treatment of comorbid conditions prior to <u>surgery</u>

* Adequate preoperative measures to prevent abdominal infection (e.g., <u>antibiotic prophylaxis</u>, intestinal cleansing )





### Emergency <u>surgery</u>




The acute onset of severe illness requiring emergency <u>surgery</u> typically means that preoperative conditions cannot be optimized (see above). This can considerably increase the risk for intraoperative and <u>postoperative complications</u>.



* Measures to prevent complications: in a two-stage surgical procedure, a temporary <u>stoma</u> is created in a first step to divert stool from diseased portions of the bowel, allowing rest, and is reversed in a second step after healing has occurred. 

* <u>Bowel resection</u> with primary anastomosis (preserving intestinal continuity)

* Creation of a protective <u>loop stoma</u>

* Bowel restoration at time of <u>stoma</u> reversal (6–8 weeks following <u>primary anastomosis</u>)

* Alternative approach: Hartmann procedure 

* <u>Bowel resection</u> and creation of an <u>end stoma</u> with an <u>artificial anus</u> if <u>primary anastomosis</u> is not possible

* Surgical re-<u>anastomosis</u> with restoration of intestinal continuity (∼ 6 months following initial operation)




![Hartmann's procedure](media/slqy5qf8js4y90p8h5lr56lc.jpg)

Hartmann's procedure




### Stoma (<u>enterostomy</u>, <u>artificial bowel outlet</u>, <u>artificial anus</u>) [[1]](/library/QxXuwZ0)




* Indication: allows removal of feces from the body

* Procedure

* The site of the <u>stoma</u> is selected and marked prior to <u>surgery</u>

* The protruding bowel is secured by a support ring to prevent it from slipping back through the <u>incision</u>.

* A <u>skin</u> barrier that allows for attaching the collection bag is fitted over and around the <u>stoma</u>.





![Healthy stoma (ostomy)](media/orp9h67yo23l1u84wjcw02bm.jpg)

Healthy stoma (ostomy)




#### Loop stoma




* Indications

* Protective <u>loop stoma</u>: protects distally located parts of the intestine (e.g., inflamed parts, fresh <u>anastomoses</u>)

* Palliative <u>loop stoma</u>: fecal drainage (e.g., cases of <u>distal</u> <u>bowel obstruction</u>)

* Technique

* Entire loop of bowel is exteriorized

* Usually, parts of the <u>ileum</u> are used (<u>ileostoma</u>).

* Handling: the <u>stoma</u> continually drains bowel contents, requiring continuous use of a <u>stoma</u> bag.

* A protective <u>loop stoma</u> is reversed a few weeks/months following <u>surgery</u> (after sufficient healing of the <u>anastomosis</u>).





![Indications for a loop stoma](media/hgud7lgytlkym70dyfebrm97.jpg)

Indications for a loop stoma

![Comparison of stoma types](media/uyplq2sstwnf29spct8k7xcb.jpg)

Comparison of stoma types

![Stoma bag](media/pg31f2dvgb9ybi8hiez92ztk.jpg)

Stoma bag




#### End stoma




* Technique 

* Exteriorization of the <u>proximal</u> end of the bowel. The <u>distal</u> end is sutured or stapled closed and remains as a blind pouch in the abdomen.

* The bowel is pulled out 1–2 cm and then sutured to the <u>skin</u>.

* Usually, parts of the <u>colon</u> (<u>colostomy</u>) are used.

* Indications

* An <u>end stoma</u> is created for incontinent patients (acts as an <u>artificial anus</u>)

* <u>Hartmann procedure</u>

* Handling [[2]](/library/cR0aNf)

* In <u>colostomy</u> patients, <u>irrigation</u> is an option (controlled evacuation of the bowel to have a period free of output, restoring control)

* <u>Irrigation</u> involves a lavage of the bowel via the <u>stoma</u> to allow for controlled fecal drainage with subsequent temporary removal of the collection bag and coverage of the <u>stoma</u> with a <u>stoma</u> cap or plug (up to 24–48 hours).

* This enables the patient to participate in activities (e.g. sports) in which a <u>stoma</u> bag would be inconvenient.

* In <u>ileostomy</u>, <u>irrigation</u> is pointless, since bowel contents are drained continuously rather than intermittently from the <u>small bowel</u>.

* Depending on the indications for the initial operation and the underlying condition, re-<u>anastomosis</u> with restoration of intestinal continuity may be possible 3–4 months following <u>surgery</u>.





![Hartmann's procedure](media/slqy5qf8js4y90p8h5lr56lc.jpg)

Hartmann's procedure

![Ileostoma](media/uttifrki9fl44h052zqx90n6.jpg)

## Complications

* General <u>postoperative complications</u>, e.g., <u>postoperative hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Surgical wound-related complications</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Surgical site infection</u>

* <u>Wound dehiscence</u>

* <u>Fascial dehiscence</u>

* <u>Postoperative ileus</u>

* <u>Anastomosis insufficiency</u> (<u>anastomotic leak</u>)

* <u>Bowel obstruction</u>, e.g., due to:

* <u>Anastomotic stricture</u>

* <u>Intestinal adhesions</u>

* <u>Fecal incontinence</u>, increased stool frequency

* <u>Ostomy complications</u>, e.g., <u>stoma</u> <u>retraction</u> or prolapse





![Wound dehiscence after inguinal hernia repair](media/yzg9b0ia85ic4ll5905covh6.jpg)

Wound dehiscence after inguinal hernia repair

![Strangulated bowel](media/frvopplvat109fb28bahc0ky.jpg)

Strangulated bowel

![Stoma complications](media/yvgo1k3j270736wmk74cd917.jpg)

Stoma complications




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Fascial dehiscence

### Definition [[3]](/library/xd1EHf0)




* The separation of a fascial closure following abdominal <u>surgery</u> due to, e.g., increased <u>intraabdominal pressure</u> or wound infection

* Partial <u>fascial dehiscence</u>: partial failure of <u>incision</u> sutures, e.g., deep sutures have failed but <u>superficial</u> <u>skin</u> sutures are intact.

* Complete <u>fascial dehiscence</u>: failure of sutures at all layers of the <u>incision</u>





### <u>Risk factors</u> [[3]](/library/xd1EHf0)[[4]](/library/HC1KtQ0)




* Postoperative intraabdominal infection

* <u>Wound healing</u> disorders

* Poor <u>suturing</u> technique

* <u>Surgical site infection</u>

* Increased <u>intraabdominal pressure</u>, e.g., due to distention or <u>coughing</u>

* Patient-related factors: <u>malnutrition</u>, advanced age, <u>obesity</u>, <u>immunosuppression</u>





### Clinical features [[3]](/library/xd1EHf0)




* Most commonly occurs 6–12 days after <u>surgery</u> [[3]](/library/xd1EHf0)[[5]](/library/Px1W9Q0)

* Profuse serosanguinous drainage

* Possible “popping” or tearing sensation

* Bulge during <u>Valsalva maneuvers</u>

* Visibly protruding intestine in complete <u>fascial dehiscence</u>

* Clinical features of other complications, e.g., intraabdominal infection





### Diagnostics




* Primarily a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>

* Consider imaging if there is diagnostic uncertainty: e.g., CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u>





### Treatment [[3]](/library/xd1EHf0)[[6]](/library/2x1TDQ0)




* Interim management

* Cover wound with moist dressing.

* Use adhesive tapes and abdominal binders to prevent further <u>wound dehiscence</u>.

* Definitive treatment: urgent surgical revision with <u>debridement</u> and reapproximation of the fascial edges





### Complications




* Organ evisceration: protrusion of abdominal organs through the outer abdomen

* Intraabdominal <u>sepsis</u>

* <u>Incisional hernia</u>





> [!WARNING]
> The risk of mortality in <u>fascial dehiscence</u> after <u>laparotomy</u> is up to 35%. [[3]](/library/xd1EHf0)




### Prevention [[3]](/library/xd1EHf0)[[6]](/library/2x1TDQ0)




* <u>Preoperative preparation</u>: e.g., <u>nutrition support</u>, <u>smoking cessation</u>

* Good surgical technique

* Avoidance of heavy lifting for 4–6 weeks after <u>laparotomy</u>  [[7]](/library/Ux1bDQ0)

## Bariatric surgery

### Indications [[17]](/library/08WeOM0)




* <u>BMI</u> ≥ 35 kg/m<sup>2</sup>

* <u>BMI</u> 30–34.9 kg/m<sup>2</sup> with either of the following:

* <u>Type 2 diabetes mellitus</u>

* Lack of improvement following nonsurgical interventions





### Procedures [[18]](/library/QKXuT_)[[19]](/library/lKXvg_)[[20]](/library/mKXVS_)




* Restrictive procedures [[21]](/library/b6XHj_)

* Goal: Reduce <u>stomach</u> volume and limit oral intake.

* Examples: <u>sleeve gastrectomy</u> (most common form of <u>bariatric surgery</u>), <u>adjustable gastric banding</u>

* Malabsorptive procedures  [[19]](/library/lKXvg_)[[21]](/library/b6XHj_)

* Goal: bypass portions of the <u>small intestine</u>, thereby impairing absorption of <u>macronutrients</u>

* Example: <u>Roux-en-Y</u> <u>gastric bypass</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Bariatric surgery</u> is an effective treatment for <u>obesity</u> and <u>metabolic syndrome</u>; however, clinicians must weigh these benefits against the risks associated with <u>surgery</u>.




### Complications [[10]](/library/UP1bVS0)[[22]](/library/Jocs1W0)




* General <u>complications of bowel surgery</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Anastomotic leaks</u>

* Strictures

* <u>Internal hernias</u>

* Procedure-specific complications, e.g.:

* <u>Esophagitis</u> and acid reflux in <u>sleeve gastrectomy</u>

* Marginal <u>ulceration</u>, gastrogastric <u>fistula</u>, <u>dumping syndrome</u>, and <u>choledocholithiasis</u> in <u>Roux-en-Y</u> bypass

* Esophageal or <u>gastric perforation</u> and band slippage in gastric <u>banding</u>

* Acute management

* <u>ABCDE survey</u>, <u>NPO</u>, <u>emergency preoperative diagnostics</u>, surgical consult

* Imaging: <u>CXR</u> and abdominal <u>x-ray</u>  and/or CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV and oral contrast

* Further measures depend on the underlying condition, e.g., <u>broad-spectrum antibiotics</u> if a leak is suspected.





> [!WARNING]
> Do not attempt <u>nasogastric tube insertion</u> without consulting the surgical team because altered anatomy increases the risk of injury from a blind insertion.




> [!TIP]
> Consider nongastrointestinal etiologies for abdominal <u>pain</u>, such as <u>myocardial infarction</u>, because bariatric patients may have additional comorbidities such as <u>coronary artery disease</u>. [[23]](/library/eP1xdS0)
